relations.note: Missionaries increasingly equated the morally variable supay category with the Christian Devil.
Bolivian miners sometimes identify Supay with the subterranean owner of ore and wealth.

relations.myth: Transformation of Tiw into the Diablada devil
relations.note: Oruro heritage narratives connect Tiw with the festival figure later called Devil or Supay.
Regional usage sometimes substitutes Saqra for Supay, although early lexicography distinguishes them.
This Aymara dangerous place-being is sometimes equated with the Devil or Supay-like mine spirits.
Some mining accounts describe Pachamama and Tío or Supay as spouses, but this is not universal.
Mine rites may address both beings as complementary or distinct recipients of offerings.
Tío or Supay may be understood as an underground aspect or transformed form of mountain ownership.
Festival devils identified loosely with Supay dance devotionally before the Virgin and submit to Marian order.
Michael defeats or disciplines Lucifer and the devils, sometimes loosely interpreted as Supay.
relations.source: Narración de los siete pecados capitales

relations.note: Festival usage sometimes overlaps Lucifer with Supay, though other versions keep their roles distinct.
Some Oruro variants connect the underground Huari with the Devil or Supay.
Supay as the Christian Devil is a subordinate enemy and fallen spirit under divine judgment.
One Potosí origin narrative says God expelled the Devil underground to possess mineral riches.
One mining narrative says dead colonial laborers became Tíos or joined the subterranean master.
Saints and Christian invocations protect mines or restrain Supay-like subterranean danger.
